decks.title: Anatomy of Flowering Plants — Part 1: Meristems, permanent tissues and tissue systems
goals: Classify meristems as apical, intercalary and lateral and state their roles
Compare parenchyma, collenchyma and sclerenchyma and name the elements of xylem and phloem
Describe the epidermal, ground and vascular tissue systems

slides.heading: Anatomy of flowering plants
slides.body_md: Part 1 — how a plant grows, and the tissues that make up its body.

visual.alt: Meristematic tissue gives permanent tissues, which form tissue systems and organs

slides.narration: Anatomy is the study of internal structure. A plant starts as dividing cells in meristems. These cells mature into permanent tissues, the tissues are grouped into three tissue systems, and the systems make up roots, stems and leaves.

slides.heading: Meristematic tissue
slides.body_md: **Meristems** are regions of cells that keep dividing. Their cells are small, thin-walled and closely packed, with dense cytoplasm, a large nucleus and very small vacuoles.

rows: Easy to divide and to expand
Cell is actively making new material

visual.alt: Table of the characteristics of meristematic cells with reasons

slides.narration: A meristematic cell is built for dividing. It has dense cytoplasm and a big nucleus, a thin wall, hardly any vacuole, and no gaps between neighbouring cells.

slides.heading: Apical, intercalary and lateral meristems
slides.body_md: By origin, meristems are **primary** (apical and intercalary) or **secondary** (lateral). By position: **apical** at tips, **intercalary** between mature tissues, **lateral** along the sides.

visual.alt: Apical, intercalary and lateral meristems

slides.narration: Apical meristems at the tips of roots and shoots make the plant longer. Intercalary meristems, found at the base of leaves and above the nodes of grasses, also add length. Lateral meristems, the vascular cambium and cork cambium, add to the girth of the stem and root.

slides.heading: Quick check: meristems
slides.body_md: Which meristem is responsible for the increase in thickness of a stem?
slides.narration: Quick check. Does the tissue add length or girth?

slides.heading: Worked example 1: growth from meristems
slides.body_md: (a) The cells of an apical meristem divide every 8 hours. Starting from one cell, how many cells are there after 48 hours? (b) An intercalary meristem at the base of a bamboo internode adds 3 cm a day. How much length is added in 12 days?
bullets: (a) Divisions = 48 ÷ 8 = 6. Each division doubles the cells, so 2^6 = **64** cells.

visual.alt: Worked table: 64 cells and 36 centimetres

slides.narration: First find the number of divisions by dividing the time by the interval. Every division doubles the number of cells, so six divisions give sixty-four cells. For the bamboo, multiply the daily growth by the number of days.

slides.heading: Simple permanent tissues
slides.body_md: Permanent tissues have stopped dividing. **Simple** tissues are made of one kind of cell.

slides.narration: Parenchyma has thin-walled living cells with spaces between them. Collenchyma has living cells with thick corners. Sclerenchyma has dead cells with thick lignified walls and a very narrow cavity.

slides.heading: Parenchyma, collenchyma and sclerenchyma compared
slides.body_md: Compare wall, living or dead state, location and function.

rows: Thickened at the corners with cellulose and pectin
Below the epidermis of dicot stems and leaf stalks
Fibres in stems, stone cells in fruits and seed coats

visual.alt: Table comparing parenchyma, collenchyma and sclerenchyma

slides.narration: Parenchyma stores food and carries out photosynthesis. Collenchyma gives flexible support to young stems and leaf stalks. Sclerenchyma is dead and rigid, and gives strength, as in fibres and in the gritty stone cells of fruits.

slides.heading: Complex tissues: xylem and phloem
slides.body_md: **Complex** tissues have more than one kind of cell working together. Xylem carries water and minerals; phloem carries food.

visual.alt: Elements of xylem and phloem

slides.narration: Xylem has tracheids, vessels, fibres and parenchyma. All but the parenchyma are dead. Phloem has sieve tube elements, companion cells, parenchyma and fibres. The sieve tube elements have no nucleus, and the companion cells beside them have one.

slides.heading: Elements of xylem and phloem
slides.body_md: Each element has a job, and most xylem elements are dead.

visual.alt: Table of the elements of xylem and phloem

slides.narration: Remember which elements are dead. In xylem the tracheids, vessels and fibres are dead; only the parenchyma lives. In phloem only the fibres are dead. The sieve tube element lives without a nucleus, with help from its companion cell.

slides.heading: Quick check: complex tissues
slides.body_md: Which cell controls the working of a sieve tube element?
slides.narration: Quick check. Which neighbouring living cell has a nucleus?

slides.heading: Worked example 2: counting vascular elements
slides.body_md: A dicot stem has a ring of 12 vascular bundles. Each has 6 vessels and 9 sieve tube elements. How many vessels and sieve tube elements are there in the ring? Of the four elements of xylem and the four of phloem, how many are dead?
bullets: Sieve tube elements = 12 × 9 = **108**.
Dead elements: xylem 3 (tracheid, vessel, fibre) and phloem 1 (fibre), so **4** in all.

visual.alt: Worked table: 72 vessels, 108 sieve tube elements, 4 dead kinds

slides.narration: Multiply the number of bundles by the number of elements in each. For the dead elements, count the three dead kinds in xylem and the one dead kind in phloem, which makes four.

slides.heading: The three tissue systems
slides.body_md: Tissues are grouped by structure and position into **epidermal**, **ground** and **vascular** systems.

rows: Epidermis, cuticle, stomata, root hairs, trichomes
All tissues except epidermis and vascular bundles
Cortex, pericycle, pith, medullary rays; mesophyll in leaves
Xylem, phloem and, in dicots, cambium

visual.alt: Table of the epidermal, ground and vascular tissue systems

slides.narration: The epidermal system is the outer skin with stomata, root hairs and trichomes. The ground system is everything between the skin and the vascular bundles. The vascular system is the xylem and phloem that conduct water and food.

slides.heading: Quick check: tissue systems
slides.body_md: To which tissue system does the pith of a stem belong?
slides.narration: Quick check. Is the pith part of the skin, the conducting tissue, or neither?

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Meristems: apical and intercalary (length), lateral (girth); small thin-walled cells with dense cytoplasm.
Simple tissues: parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma.
Complex tissues: xylem (tracheid, vessel, fibre, parenchyma) and phloem (sieve tube, companion cell, parenchyma, fibre).
Tissue systems: epidermal, ground, vascular.

visual.alt: Summary table of tissues and key points

slides.narration: To recap: meristems divide and make the plant longer or thicker, permanent tissues are simple or complex, and the tissues are grouped into the epidermal, ground and vascular systems.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Give **wall, living or dead, location and function** when comparing simple tissues.
Name which xylem elements are **dead**.
Say that sieve tube elements have **no nucleus** and are helped by companion cells.
Place the **pith and cortex** in the ground tissue system.
slides.narration: Exam tips. When comparing simple tissues give the wall, whether the cell is alive, where it is found and what it does. Name the dead xylem elements. Remember that sieve tubes lack a nucleus. And place the cortex and pith in the ground system.

decks.title: Anatomy of Flowering Plants — Part 2: Roots, stems and leaves
goals: Draw and label transverse sections of dicot and monocot roots and stems
List the anatomical differences between dicot and monocot roots and stems
Draw and label vertical sections of a dicot and a monocot leaf

slides.heading: Organs of a flowering plant
slides.body_md: Part 2 — how the tissues are arranged in roots, stems and leaves.

visual.alt: Root, stem and leaf as the three organs studied

slides.narration: Cut across a root, a stem or a leaf and look through a microscope. The same three tissue systems are there, but they are arranged differently in each organ, and differently again in dicots and monocots.

slides.heading: Dicot root
slides.body_md: From outside in: **epiblema**, wide **cortex**, **endodermis** with Casparian strips, **pericycle**, **vascular bundles** with few xylem arms, and a small pith.

visual.spec: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 540 330" role="img" aria-label="Transverse section of a dicot root: a single outer layer, the epiblema, some cells of which bear root hairs; a wide cortex of parenchyma with spaces between the cells; the endodermis, a ring of barrel-shaped cells with Casparian strips; the pericycle just inside it; and the vascular cylinder in the centre with four xylem arms alternating with four patches of phloem, separated by conjunctive tissue, with the oldest xylem (protoxylem) towards the outside of each arm and a very small pith" visual.alt: Transverse section of a dicot root

slides.narration: The outer layer is the epiblema, with root hairs. The cortex is thick parenchyma. The endodermis has waterproof Casparian strips. Inside is the pericycle and then two to four xylem arms alternating with phloem, a radial arrangement. The pith is small.

slides.heading: Monocot root
slides.body_md: The same layers are present, but there are **more than six** xylem arms and a **large pith**.

visual.alt: Transverse section of a monocot root

slides.narration: The monocot root has the same layers as the dicot root. The difference is that it has many xylem arms, more than six, which is called polyarch, and a large pith in the centre. It does not show secondary growth.

slides.heading: Dicot and monocot roots compared
slides.body_md: Three points are usually asked.

visual.alt: Table comparing dicot and monocot roots

slides.narration: Compare the number of xylem arms, the size of the pith and the secondary growth. The dicot root has few arms, a small pith and secondary growth. The monocot root has many arms, a large pith and none.

slides.heading: Quick check: roots
slides.body_md: A root section shows eight xylem arms and a large pith. What kind of root is it?
slides.narration: Quick check. Count the xylem arms.

slides.heading: Dicot stem
slides.body_md: Epidermis, **collenchymatous hypodermis**, cortex, endodermis, pericycle, **vascular bundles in a ring** (conjoint, open), medullary rays and a **pith**.

visual.alt: Transverse section of a dicot stem

slides.narration: In the dicot stem the bundles form a ring. Each is conjoint and open, with phloem outside, a strip of cambium, and xylem inside, the protoxylem lying towards the pith. Medullary rays run between the bundles, and a large pith lies in the centre.

slides.heading: Monocot stem
slides.body_md: Sclerenchymatous hypodermis; **scattered** conjoint, **closed** bundles in parenchymatous ground tissue; **no** medullary rays or pith.

visual.alt: Transverse section of a monocot stem

slides.narration: In the monocot stem the bundles are scattered through the ground tissue, smaller and more crowded near the edge. Each is closed, with no cambium, and is wrapped in a sclerenchyma sheath. There is no phloem parenchyma and no separate pith.

slides.heading: Dicot and monocot stems compared
slides.body_md: Compare the arrangement and type of bundles, the hypodermis and the ground tissue.

visual.alt: Table comparing dicot and monocot stems

slides.narration: Dicot stems have bundles in a ring, with cambium, a collenchyma hypodermis, medullary rays and pith. Monocot stems have scattered closed bundles, a sclerenchyma hypodermis and undifferentiated ground tissue.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: strands and pith area
slides.body_md: (a) A wheat root has 14 xylem bundles alternating with phloem bundles. How many vascular strands are there? (b) A stem section has a radius of 3 mm and its pith has a radius of 1.2 mm. What percentage of the area of the section is the pith?
bullets: (a) Phloem bundles alternate, so there are 14 of them too: 14 + 14 = **28** strands.
(b) Area is proportional to the square of the radius: (1.2 ÷ 3)² × 100 = **16 percent**.

visual.alt: Worked table: 28 strands and 16 percent

slides.narration: In a root, phloem alternates with xylem, so the number of phloem bundles equals the number of xylem bundles. For the area, remember that area depends on the square of the radius, so divide the radii, square, and multiply by one hundred.

slides.heading: Quick check: stems
slides.body_md: A stem section shows scattered closed bundles. What kind of stem is it?
slides.narration: Quick check. Are the bundles in a ring, or scattered?

slides.heading: Dicot leaf (dorsiventral)
slides.body_md: Upper epidermis, **palisade** parenchyma, **spongy** parenchyma with air spaces, lower epidermis with more **stomata**; the bundle has xylem towards the upper side.

visual.alt: Vertical section of a dicot leaf

slides.narration: In a dicot leaf the palisade cells are tall and packed just below the upper surface. The spongy cells below are loosely arranged with air spaces. Most stomata are in the lower epidermis, each with two guard cells over a sub-stomatal cavity.

slides.heading: Monocot leaf (isobilateral)
slides.body_md: Similar epidermis on both sides, **bulliform cells**, mesophyll **not differentiated**, stomata on **both** surfaces.

slides.narration: In the monocot leaf the two surfaces look alike, and stomata are found on both. The mesophyll is one kind of cell, not divided into palisade and spongy tissue. Large bulliform cells in the upper epidermis help the leaf to roll in dry weather.

slides.heading: Dorsiventral and isobilateral leaves compared
slides.body_md: Four points distinguish the two kinds of leaf.

visual.alt: Table comparing dorsiventral and isobilateral leaves

slides.narration: A dorsiventral leaf has different upper and lower sides, with palisade and spongy mesophyll and more stomata below. An isobilateral leaf has similar sides, one kind of mesophyll, stomata on both sides and bulliform cells.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: counting stomata
slides.body_md: A mango leaf has 250 stomata per square millimetre on its lower surface, which measures 30 square centimetres, and none on the upper. A paddy leaf has 90 per square millimetre on each surface, one surface measuring 12 square centimetres. Find the stomata on each leaf.
bullets: Paddy: 12 cm² = 1200 mm²; 90 × 1200 = 108000 per surface, so **216000** on both.

visual.alt: Worked table: 750000 stomata in the mango leaf and 216000 in the paddy leaf

slides.narration: First change the area to square millimetres by multiplying by one hundred. Then multiply by the density. In the mango only the lower surface counts. In the paddy leaf both surfaces carry stomata, so double the count for one surface.

slides.heading: Quick check: leaves
slides.body_md: In a leaf section the mesophyll is a single kind of cell and the epidermis has bulliform cells. Which leaf is it?
slides.narration: Quick check. Is there a palisade layer?

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Root: epiblema, cortex, endodermis, pericycle, radial bundles; dicot few xylem arms and small pith, monocot many arms and large pith.
Stem: dicot bundles in a ring, open, collenchymatous hypodermis, pith; monocot bundles scattered, closed, sclerenchymatous hypodermis.
Leaf: dicot palisade and spongy mesophyll, more stomata below; monocot undifferentiated mesophyll, bulliform cells, stomata on both sides.

visual.alt: Summary table of dicot and monocot organs

slides.narration: To recap: roots have a radial arrangement of xylem and phloem, with more arms in monocots. Dicot stems have bundles in a ring and monocot stems have them scattered. Dicot leaves have palisade and spongy tissue, monocot leaves do not.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Draw the layers **in order** from the outside and label at least six.
Write differences as **points in a table**, one feature per row.
Name **open** and **closed** bundles with the presence of cambium.
Mention **bulliform cells** for a monocot leaf.

notes.title: Anatomy of Flowering Plants — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Meristematic tissues
sections.body_md:
**Anatomy** is the study of the internal structure of an organism. Plant growth is localised: it takes place in **meristems**, groups of cells that retain the power of division.

**Characteristics of meristematic cells:** small, thin-walled (primary wall only), closely packed with **no intercellular spaces**, dense cytoplasm, a prominent nucleus and very small or no vacuoles.

**Classification by origin.** **Primary** meristems arise from the embryo and are present from the beginning (apical and intercalary). **Secondary** meristems arise later from permanent tissue that becomes meristematic again (the cambia).

**Classification by position.**
- **Apical meristems** at the tips of roots and shoots: they add **length** (primary growth).
- **Intercalary meristems** between mature tissues, at the bases of leaves and above the nodes of grasses: they add length and allow regrowth of grazed grass.
- **Lateral meristems** (vascular cambium and cork cambium) along the sides of stem and root: they add **girth** (secondary growth).

key_terms.definition_md: A region of cells that keeps dividing.
Meristem at the tip of a root or shoot; adds length.
Meristem at the base of an internode or leaf; adds length.
Cambium; adds girth.

sections.heading: 2. Permanent tissues
sections.body_md:
Cells produced by meristems mature and lose the power of division; they form **permanent tissues**.

**Simple tissues** have one kind of cell.
- **Parenchyma** — living cells with **thin cellulose walls**, usually rounded, with intercellular spaces. Found in the cortex, pith, mesophyll and fruits. Functions: storage, photosynthesis (as chlorenchyma), secretion, and buoyancy in water plants (aerenchyma).
- **Collenchyma** — living cells with walls **unevenly thickened at the corners** with cellulose and pectin. Found below the epidermis of dicot stems and in leaf stalks. Function: mechanical support to **growing** parts, with flexibility.
- **Sclerenchyma** — **dead** cells with thick, **lignified** walls and a narrow lumen: **fibres** (long, pointed) and **sclereids** (stone cells; in fruits such as guava and in seed coats). Function: mechanical strength.

**Complex tissues** have more than one kind of cell that work together.
- **Xylem** conducts **water and minerals**. Elements: **tracheids**, **vessels**, **xylem fibres** (all dead) and **xylem parenchyma** (living).
- **Phloem** conducts **food**. Elements: **sieve tube elements** (living, with no nucleus at maturity, sieve plates at their end walls), **companion cells** (living, with a nucleus; control the sieve tube), **phloem parenchyma** and **phloem fibres** (dead).

*Where books differ.* Some books say that phloem parenchyma is absent in most monocots; the notes state that for the monocot stem only.

key_terms.definition_md: Living cells with corners thickened by cellulose and pectin.
Dead cells with thick lignified walls.
A dead water-conducting tube of cells joined end to end.
Nucleated living cell beside a sieve tube element.

sections.heading: 3. Tissue systems
sections.body_md:
Tissues are grouped into three systems by their structure and position.
- **Epidermal tissue system** — the **epidermis** (usually a single layer of closely packed cells, often with a waxy **cuticle**), **stomata** (two guard cells around a pore), **root hairs** (unicellular outgrowths of the epidermis of the root, called **epiblema**) and **trichomes** (hairs on shoots).
- **Ground tissue system** — all tissues except the epidermis and the vascular bundles: **cortex, pericycle, pith and medullary rays** in stems and roots; the **mesophyll** (palisade and spongy parenchyma) in leaves.
- **Vascular tissue system** — **xylem and phloem**; in dicots a strip of **cambium** lies between them in the bundle. Bundles are **radial** (xylem and phloem on different radii, alternating, as in roots) or **conjoint** (xylem and phloem on the same radius, as in stems and leaves); conjoint bundles are **open** (with cambium) or **closed** (without).

sections.heading: 4. Internal structure of roots and stems (T.S.)
sections.body_md:
**Dicot root.** From outside: **epiblema** (with root hairs), **cortex** (thin-walled parenchyma with intercellular spaces), **endodermis** (one layer of barrel-shaped cells with **Casparian strips** of suberin on radial walls), **pericycle** (thin-walled; gives rise to lateral roots and to cambium during secondary growth), **vascular bundles** — radial, with **two to four** xylem arms alternating with phloem patches, with **conjunctive tissue** between them — and a **small or absent pith**. Xylem is **exarch** (protoxylem towards the periphery).

**Monocot root.** The same layers, but **more than six** xylem arms (polyarch) and a **large, well-developed pith**; no secondary growth.

**Dicot stem.** **Epidermis** (with trichomes), **hypodermis** of **collenchyma**, **cortex** of parenchyma, **endodermis** (the starch sheath), **pericycle** (often patches of sclerenchyma over the bundles), **medullary rays** and a large **pith**. The vascular bundles are **in a ring**, **conjoint, collateral and open** (cambium between phloem and xylem), with **endarch** xylem (protoxylem towards the pith).

**Monocot stem.** **Sclerenchymatous hypodermis**; **ground tissue not differentiated** into cortex, pericycle, medullary rays and pith; **many scattered bundles**, smaller and more crowded near the periphery, each **conjoint and closed** (no cambium) and wrapped in a **sclerenchymatous bundle sheath**; **no phloem parenchyma**; often with water-containing cavities (protoxylem lacuna).

| Feature | Dicot root | Monocot root |
|---|---|---|
| Xylem arms | Two to four | More than six |
| Pith | Small or absent | Large |
| Secondary growth | Present | Absent |

| Feature | Dicot stem | Monocot stem |
|---|---|---|
| Bundles | In a ring | Scattered |
| Cambium | Present (open) | Absent (closed) |
| Hypodermis | Collenchyma | Sclerenchyma |
| Pith and medullary rays | Present | Absent |

sections.heading: 5. Internal structure of leaves (V.S.)
sections.body_md:
**Dicot (dorsiventral) leaf.** **Upper epidermis** with a cuticle; **mesophyll** of **palisade parenchyma** (one or two layers of tall, closely packed, chloroplast-rich cells under the upper epidermis) and **spongy parenchyma** (loosely arranged, rounded cells with large air spaces); **lower epidermis** with more **stomata**. Each stoma has two bean-shaped **guard cells** and lies over a **sub-stomatal cavity**. **Vascular bundles** are surrounded by a **bundle sheath** of parenchyma; the xylem is towards the upper surface and the phloem towards the lower. Venation is reticulate.

**Monocot (isobilateral) leaf.** Similar on both sides: **stomata on both surfaces** in about equal numbers; **mesophyll not differentiated** into palisade and spongy; large thin-walled **bulliform cells** in groups in the upper epidermis, which help the leaf roll inwards in dry weather by losing water; **parallel venation**, the bundles of similar size with sclerenchyma above and below.

| Feature | Dicot leaf | Monocot leaf |
|---|---|---|
| Mesophyll | Palisade and spongy | Not differentiated |
| Stomata | More below | About equal on both |
| Bulliform cells | Absent | Present |

key_terms.definition_md: Tall, closely packed photosynthetic cells under the upper epidermis.
Loosely arranged mesophyll cells with air spaces.
Large epidermal cells that help a grass leaf to roll.
Pair of cells that surround a stoma.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Saying that lateral meristems add length; they add girth.
- Writing that collenchyma is dead or lignified; it is living, with cellulose and pectin.
- Saying that all xylem elements are dead; the xylem parenchyma lives.
- Saying that sieve tube elements have a nucleus; it is the companion cell that has one.
- Giving the monocot stem a ring of bundles or cambium.
- Placing the pith or cortex in the vascular system; both belong to the ground tissue system.
- Drawing a leaf section with no bundle sheath or with the phloem on the upper side.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark subparts: a meristem, an element of xylem or phloem, open or closed, a lettered figure, a give-a-reason.
- 2- and 3-mark questions: parenchyma against collenchyma; xylem against phloem; dicot against monocot stem; the endodermis.
- 5-mark questions in parts: a labelled diagram of a T.S. of a stem, root or leaf, with differences.

cards.back_md: A region of cells that keeps dividing.
Small, thin wall, dense cytoplasm, big nucleus, no intercellular spaces.
Base of leaves, above the nodes of grasses.
Thickened at corners with cellulose and pectin; living.
Sieve tube elements, companion cells, parenchyma, fibres.
Absent at maturity; companion cell controls it.

Xylem arms in a monocot root?

cards.back_md: In a ring; conjoint and open.

cards.front_md: Two kinds of mesophyll in a dicot leaf?
Which cells help a grass leaf to roll?
Stomata in dicot versus monocot leaf?
cards.back_md: More on the lower surface versus about equal on both.

questions.stem_md: Over several years a tree trunk becomes much thicker. The tissue responsible for this increase in girth is the
questions.solution_md: Lateral meristems, the vascular cambium and cork cambium, add to the girth — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A student nips off the extreme tip of a young root with a blade. The root stops lengthening because the
questions.solution_md: Cell division that lengthens a root takes place in its apical meristem — option (d).

questions.stem_md: The internodes of a bamboo shoot go on lengthening from their bases even after the shoot tip has been cut off. This is possible because of the
questions.solution_md: Intercalary meristems at the bases of internodes add length — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The cells of a meristem are closely packed with no intercellular spaces.

**Reason (R):** Meristematic cells have thick lignified walls.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: A is true. R is false: meristematic cells have thin primary walls, and lignified walls belong to sclerenchyma — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between apical and lateral meristems on their position and on the kind of growth each brings about.

answer.model_answer_md: **Apical** meristems lie at the **tips of roots and shoots** and increase the **length** of the plant (primary growth). **Lateral** meristems, the vascular cambium and cork cambium, lie along the **sides** of stem and root and increase their **girth** (secondary growth).

questions.stem_md: The cells of a root-tip meristem divide once every 4 hours. Starting from one cell, how many cells are there after 20 hours?

(a) Name the three kinds of meristem according to position and state where each is found. [3]
(b) A grass plant is grazed to the ground but grows again within days. Explain why. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Apical** meristems lie at the **tips of roots and shoots**; **intercalary** meristems lie at the **bases of leaves and internodes**; **lateral** meristems, the vascular cambium and cork cambium, lie along the **sides** of stems and roots.

(b) The leaves of grass grow from an **intercalary meristem** at their **bases**, which lie near the ground and are not removed by grazing. Its cells keep **dividing and elongating**, so the leaf **regrows** quickly.

questions.stem_md: The ridges of a young pumpkin stem are firm yet flexible. Under the microscope the cells just below the epidermis are living and have corners thickened with cellulose and pectin. The tissue is
questions.solution_md: Living cells with thickened corners form collenchyma — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A guava has gritty particles in its flesh. They are groups of cells with very thick, lignified walls and a narrow cavity. These cells are
questions.solution_md: Stone cells (sclereids) are dead cells of sclerenchyma — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The long, strong fibres obtained from the jute stem and used for making ropes are mainly
questions.solution_md: Fibres are elongated sclerenchyma cells with lignified walls — option (a).

questions.stem_md: The leaf stalks of a water lily have large air cavities that help them float. The tissue forming them is
questions.solution_md: Parenchyma with large air cavities is aerenchyma — option (a).

questions.stem_md: An aphid pushes its fine mouthpart into a young stem and sugary sap flows into it. The mouthpart has entered

options.text_md: sieve tube elements of the phloem

questions.solution_md: Sugary sap is carried in the sieve tubes of the phloem — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Which living cell, with a nucleus, lies beside a sieve tube element and controls its working?
questions.solution_md: The companion cell, which has a nucleus, supports the enucleate sieve tube element — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Collenchyma gives flexible support to growing parts of a plant.

**Reason (R):** Collenchyma cells are living and their walls are thickened with cellulose and pectin.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and R explains A: the living cells with cellulose-pectin thickening can support yet stretch as the organ grows — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Xylem carries water and minerals from the roots to the leaves.

**Reason (R):** Phloem carries food from the leaves to the other parts of the plant.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but R does not explain A: they describe two different tissues — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Give a reason: a sieve tube element stays alive and conducts food although it has no nucleus.

answer.model_answer_md: The nucleated companion cell beside it controls its activities.

questions.stem_md: Give a reason: sclerenchyma cells are dead at maturity.

answer.model_answer_md: Heavy lignin deposition on the walls cuts off the protoplasm from its supplies, so it dies.

questions.stem_md: Name the four elements of xylem and state which of them is living.

answer.model_answer_md: The four elements of **xylem** are **tracheids**, **vessels**, **xylem fibres** and **xylem parenchyma**. Of these, the tracheids, vessels and fibres are **dead** at maturity, and only the **xylem parenchyma** is **living**.

questions.stem_md: State the roles of the sieve tube elements and of the companion cells of phloem.

answer.model_answer_md: **Sieve tube elements** are tubes joined end to end through sieve plates and **conduct food** such as sucrose, although they have no nucleus at maturity. **Companion cells** are nucleated living cells beside them that **control** the sieve tube elements and help in loading and unloading food.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between collenchyma and sclerenchyma on the nature of the wall and on whether the cells are living.

answer.model_answer_md: In **collenchyma** the wall is **unevenly thickened at the corners** with cellulose and pectin, and the cells are **living**. In **sclerenchyma** the wall is **thick and lignified throughout**, and the cells are **dead** at maturity.

questions.stem_md: Describe the structure, the location and the functions of parenchyma.

answer.model_answer_md: **Parenchyma** is made of living cells that are usually rounded, with **thin cellulose walls** and small intercellular spaces. It is found in the **cortex and pith** of stems and roots, in the **mesophyll** of leaves and in fruits. It **stores food**, carries out **photosynthesis** when it has chloroplasts, and secretes substances.

questions.stem_md: Compare xylem and phloem on three points.

answer.model_answer_md: **Xylem** conducts **water and minerals** upward from the roots; **phloem** conducts **food** from the leaves to other parts. Xylem is made mainly of **dead** elements (tracheids, vessels, fibres), whereas **most** phloem elements are **living** (sieve tube elements, companion cells, parenchyma). Xylem has **vessels and tracheids**; phloem has **sieve tubes with sieve plates**.

questions.stem_md: A dicot stem has a ring of 15 bundles, each with 7 vessels and 11 sieve tube elements. How many vessels are there in the ring?
An aphid taking sap from the phloem of a stem collects 6 microlitres of sap every hour. How many microlitres does it collect in 9 hours?
A sample of guava flesh has 25 clusters of stone cells, each with 18 cells. How many stone cells does the sample have?

(a) Compare parenchyma, collenchyma and sclerenchyma in the nature of the wall and in function. [3]
(b) Name the two complex tissues of a plant and say which element of each is living. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Parenchyma** has **thin cellulose** walls and stores food or photosynthesises. **Collenchyma** has walls **thickened at the corners** with cellulose and pectin and gives **flexible support**. **Sclerenchyma** has **thick lignified** walls, is dead, and gives **mechanical strength**.

(b) The complex tissues are **xylem** and **phloem**. In xylem the **parenchyma** is living; in phloem the **sieve tube elements, companion cells and parenchyma** are living.

questions.solution_md: Three simple tissues; xylem and phloem.

questions.stem_md: The pith of a stem belongs to the
questions.solution_md: Pith, cortex and medullary rays are ground tissue — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Which pair of structures belongs to the epidermal tissue system?
questions.solution_md: Stomata, root hairs, trichomes and the cuticle belong to the epidermal system — option (c).

questions.stem_md: In the vascular bundles of a stem the xylem and phloem lie on the same radius. Such bundles are called
questions.solution_md: Xylem and phloem on the same radius make a conjoint bundle — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Name the three tissue systems of a flowering plant and give two parts of the ground tissue system of a stem.

answer.model_answer_md: The three tissue systems are the **epidermal**, **ground** and **vascular** tissue systems. The ground tissue system of a stem includes the **cortex**, the **pericycle**, the **pith** and the **medullary rays**.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between radial and conjoint vascular bundles, with the organ in which each is found.

answer.model_answer_md: In a **radial** bundle the xylem and phloem lie on **different radii**, alternating with each other, as in **roots**. In a **conjoint** bundle they lie together on the **same radius**, as in **stems and leaves**.

questions.stem_md: Describe the epidermal tissue system, naming three structures that belong to it and one role of each.

answer.model_answer_md: The **epidermis** is usually a single layer of closely packed cells with a waxy **cuticle** that **reduces water loss**. **Stomata**, each with two guard cells, allow **gas exchange and transpiration**. **Root hairs**, outgrowths of the root epidermis, **absorb water and minerals**, and **trichomes** on the shoot reduce water loss or protect.

questions.stem_md: A transverse section of a root shows eight xylem arms alternating with eight phloem patches, and a large pith. The root is
questions.solution_md: More than six xylem arms and a large pith are features of a monocot root — option (a).

questions.stem_md: In a transverse section of a root, bands of suberin on the radial walls of a single layer of barrel-shaped cells make water pass through their cytoplasm. This layer is the
questions.solution_md: Casparian strips are bands in the walls of the endodermis — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Lateral roots arise from the
questions.solution_md: The pericycle, a layer inside the endodermis, gives rise to lateral roots — option (c).

questions.stem_md: In a transverse section of a root, the first-formed xylem elements (protoxylem) lie

options.text_md: towards the centre, next to the pith
between the phloem and the epiblema
towards the periphery, next to the pericycle

questions.solution_md: Root xylem is exarch: protoxylem outwards, metaxylem inwards — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A transverse section of a stem shows many vascular bundles scattered through the ground tissue, each without cambium. The stem is
questions.solution_md: Scattered closed bundles belong to a monocot stem — option (a).

questions.stem_md: In a stem section each vascular bundle has phloem outside, xylem inside and a thin strip of dividing cells between them. The bundle is
questions.solution_md: A conjoint bundle with cambium is open — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A section of a sugarcane stem shows no cortex, no medullary rays and no pith, with sclerenchymatous sheaths around the bundles. These features show that the stem is
questions.solution_md: Undifferentiated ground tissue and sclerenchymatous bundle sheaths indicate a monocot stem — option (c).

questions.stem_md: In the lettered figure of a stem section, the layer that gives flexible support just below the epidermis is marked
questions.solution_md: A is the hypodermis of collenchyma — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? A monocot root usually has a large, well-developed pith.
questions.solution_md: True: a large pith is a feature of the monocot root.

questions.stem_md: The bands of suberin on the radial walls of the cells of the endodermis are called ______ strips.
Match each organ (column I) with its feature (column II).

match_right.text_md: Large pith and many xylem arms
Conjoint, open bundles in a ring

questions.solution_md: Dicot stem: open bundles in a ring; monocot stem: scattered closed bundles; dicot root: two to four arms; monocot root: large pith.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The vascular bundles of a monocot stem are closed.

**Reason (R):** There is no cambium between the xylem and the phloem of the bundles of a monocot stem.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and R explains A: a bundle without cambium is called closed — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Give a reason: water entering the vascular cylinder of a root must pass through the cytoplasm of endodermal cells.

answer.model_answer_md: The Casparian strips of suberin on their radial walls are waterproof, so water cannot pass between the cells.

marking_scheme.step: Waterproof Casparian strips on radial walls

questions.stem_md: Give a reason: a monocot stem cannot increase in girth in the way a dicot stem does.

answer.model_answer_md: Its vascular bundles are closed and have no cambium, so there is no lateral meristem to add new tissue.

questions.stem_md: State two anatomical differences between a dicot root and a monocot root.

answer.model_answer_md: A **dicot root** has **two to four** xylem arms (di- to tetrarch), whereas a **monocot root** has **more than six** (polyarch). The **pith** is **small or absent** in a dicot root and **large and well developed** in a monocot root. A dicot root also shows secondary growth, which a monocot root lacks.

questions.stem_md: State two differences between the vascular bundles of a dicot stem and those of a monocot stem.

answer.model_answer_md: In a **dicot stem** the bundles are arranged **in a ring** and are **open**, with cambium between the xylem and phloem. In a **monocot stem** the bundles are **scattered** through the ground tissue and are **closed**, with no cambium; each is also surrounded by a sclerenchymatous sheath.

questions.stem_md: What are Casparian strips? State their role in the root.

answer.model_answer_md: **Casparian strips** are bands of **suberin** on the radial and transverse walls of the cells of the **endodermis**. They are **waterproof**, so water and minerals cannot move between the cells and must pass **through their cytoplasm**, which controls what enters the vascular cylinder.

questions.stem_md: Describe the arrangement of the tissues, from the outside inwards, in a transverse section of a dicot stem up to the vascular bundles.

answer.model_answer_md: The outermost layer is the **epidermis**, often with trichomes and a cuticle. Below it is the **hypodermis** of several layers of **collenchyma**. Next comes the **cortex** of **parenchyma**, and its innermost layer is the **endodermis**, rich in starch grains (starch sheath). Inside it the **pericycle**, often patches of **sclerenchyma**, lies outside the vascular bundles.

questions.stem_md: List three anatomical features of a monocot stem as seen in transverse section.

answer.model_answer_md: A monocot stem has a **sclerenchymatous hypodermis** below the epidermis. Its **ground tissue** is not differentiated into cortex, pericycle, medullary rays and pith. The **vascular bundles** are **many and scattered**, smaller near the periphery, each **conjoint and closed** with a sclerenchymatous sheath, and **phloem parenchyma is absent**.

questions.stem_md: Describe the layers of a dicot root, from the outside inwards, up to the pericycle.

answer.model_answer_md: The outer layer is the **epiblema**, whose cells bear **root hairs**. Below it is the wide **cortex** of thin-walled **parenchyma** cells with intercellular spaces. Its innermost layer is the **endodermis**, a ring of barrel-shaped cells with **Casparian strips** on the radial walls. Next comes the **pericycle**, a layer of thin-walled cells from which lateral roots arise.

questions.stem_md: A student has two stem sections, X with a ring of bundles and a large pith and Y with scattered bundles and no pith. Identify each section and give three further differences between the two stems.

answer.model_answer_md: **X** is a **dicot** stem and **Y** a **monocot** stem. In X the hypodermis is **collenchymatous**, the bundles are **open** (with cambium) and **medullary rays** are present; in Y the hypodermis is **sclerenchymatous**, the bundles are **closed** (no cambium) and the ground tissue is **not differentiated**, with no medullary rays.

questions.stem_md: A monocot root has 10 xylem arms with an equal number of phloem patches alternating with them. How many strands of vascular tissue does it have in all?
A dicot root has 3 xylem arms. How many strands of xylem and phloem together does a transverse section show?
In a transverse section of a stem the section has a radius of 4 mm and the pith has a radius of 1 mm. What percentage of the area of the section is occupied by the pith?
A sugarcane stem section shows 40 vascular bundles. One bundle in every four is small and peripheral and the rest are central. How many central bundles are there?

(a) Draw a labelled diagram of a transverse section of a dicot stem, naming at least six parts. [3]
(b) State two differences between this stem and a monocot stem. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) A circular section: **epidermis**, **hypodermis** (collenchyma), **cortex** (parenchyma), **endodermis**, **pericycle**, **vascular bundles in a ring** each with **phloem** outside, **cambium** and **xylem** inside, **medullary rays** and a **pith**; all labelled.

(b) The dicot stem has bundles **in a ring** and **open** (cambium present); the monocot stem has bundles **scattered** and **closed**. The dicot hypodermis is **collenchymatous**, the monocot **sclerenchymatous**.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Draw a labelled diagram of a transverse section of a monocot stem, naming at least five parts. [3]
(b) Explain why the stem does not show secondary growth. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) A circular section: **epidermis**, **sclerenchymatous hypodermis**, **ground tissue** of parenchyma, and many **scattered vascular bundles**, smaller near the edge, each with a **sclerenchymatous sheath**, **xylem** inside and **phloem** outside; all labelled.

(b) The bundles are **closed** and have **no cambium** between xylem and phloem. Without a lateral meristem there is no new vascular tissue added, so the stem **cannot thicken** by secondary growth.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Draw a labelled diagram of a transverse section of a dicot root, naming at least six parts. [3]
(b) State two differences between it and a monocot root. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) A circular section: **epiblema** with **root hairs**, **cortex**, **endodermis** with **Casparian strips**, **pericycle**, **xylem arms** (two to four) alternating with **phloem** patches, **conjunctive tissue** and a very small **pith**; all labelled.

(b) A dicot root has **two to four** xylem arms and a **small or absent pith**; a monocot root has **more than six** arms and a **large pith**.

questions.stem_md: A student writes four statements about stem sections: (i) a monocot stem has a ring of open bundles; (ii) a dicot stem has bundles in a ring; (iii) a dicot stem has a hypodermis of collenchyma; (iv) a dicot root has a large pith. Which statements are correct?
questions.solution_md: A monocot stem has scattered closed bundles, so (i) is wrong; a dicot root has a small pith, so (iv) is wrong; (ii) and (iii) are correct — option (b).

questions.solution_md: Undifferentiated mesophyll and bulliform cells indicate an isobilateral monocot leaf — option (b).

questions.stem_md: In the lettered figure of a leaf section, most photosynthesis takes place in the layer marked
questions.solution_md: B is the palisade parenchyma, rich in chloroplasts and placed under the upper epidermis — option (c).

questions.stem_md: In a section of a leaf a student finds the tall, tightly packed cells with the most chloroplasts just below the
questions.solution_md: Palisade parenchyma lies just below the upper epidermis — option (b).

questions.stem_md: In dry weather the blade of a grass leaf rolls inwards, reducing water loss. This movement is brought about by the loss of water from
questions.solution_md: Large thin-walled bulliform cells of the upper epidermis lose water and become flaccid, so the blade rolls — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A leaf has most of its stomata on the lower surface, tall palisade cells below the upper epidermis and spongy tissue below them. It is
questions.solution_md: Palisade and spongy mesophyll with more stomata below mark a dorsiventral leaf — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The mesophyll of a monocot leaf is differentiated into palisade and spongy tissue.

**Reason (R):** Monocot leaves have stomata only on the lower surface.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are false: the mesophyll of a monocot leaf is not differentiated, and stomata are found on both surfaces — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Give a reason: the palisade cells are placed just below the upper epidermis of a dicot leaf.

answer.model_answer_md: Light falls on the upper surface, so the chloroplast-rich palisade cells get the most light for photosynthesis.

questions.stem_md: Give a reason: the spongy parenchyma of a leaf has large air spaces.

answer.model_answer_md: The spaces allow gases such as carbon dioxide and oxygen to move quickly between the stomata and the cells.

questions.stem_md: Describe a stoma and state its function.

answer.model_answer_md: A **stoma** is a minute **pore** in the epidermis of a leaf, bounded by two bean-shaped **guard cells** that contain chloroplasts. It lies over a **sub-stomatal cavity**. Stomata allow **exchange of gases** and the **loss of water vapour** in transpiration, and the guard cells open and close the pore.

questions.stem_md: Describe the mesophyll of a dicot leaf and the position of its vascular bundles.

answer.model_answer_md: The **mesophyll** has two parts. The **palisade parenchyma** is a layer of tall, closely packed cells with many chloroplasts under the upper epidermis. The **spongy parenchyma** below is made of loosely arranged rounded cells with large **air spaces**. The **vascular bundles** lie in the mesophyll, each with a **bundle sheath**, the xylem towards the upper surface and the phloem towards the lower.

questions.stem_md: Describe three anatomical features of a monocot leaf as seen in a vertical section.

answer.model_answer_md: The **epidermis** on both surfaces is similar and carries **stomata on both**. Groups of large thin-walled **bulliform cells** lie in the upper epidermis and help the leaf to roll. The **mesophyll** is **not differentiated** into palisade and spongy tissue, and the **vascular bundles** run parallel, each with a sheath.

questions.stem_md: A student has a leaf of mango and a leaf of paddy. Explain how a section of each would differ in the mesophyll, the distribution of stomata and the epidermis of the upper surface.

answer.model_answer_md: In the **mango** (dicot) leaf the mesophyll has **palisade and spongy** layers, stomata lie **mostly on the lower** surface, and the upper epidermis has no special large cells. In the **paddy** (monocot) leaf the mesophyll is **not differentiated**, stomata are about **equal on both** surfaces, and the upper epidermis has **bulliform cells**.

questions.stem_md: The lower surface of a leaf has an area of 40 square centimetres and carries 180 stomata per square millimetre. How many stomata are on this surface?

(a) Draw a labelled diagram of a vertical section of a dicot leaf, naming at least six parts. [3]
(b) State two ways in which a monocot leaf differs. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Upper epidermis** with cuticle; **palisade parenchyma**; **spongy parenchyma** with air spaces; **vascular bundle** with **xylem** on the upper side, **phloem** below and a **bundle sheath**; **lower epidermis** with a **stoma** and **guard cells**; all labelled.

(b) A monocot leaf has **mesophyll not differentiated** into palisade and spongy tissue, **stomata on both** surfaces and **bulliform cells** in the upper epidermis.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Draw a labelled diagram of a vertical section of a monocot leaf, naming at least five parts. [3]
(b) Explain how bulliform cells help the leaf in dry weather. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Upper and lower epidermis** with **stomata** on both; groups of **bulliform cells** in the upper epidermis; undifferentiated **mesophyll**; **vascular bundles** with **bundle sheath**, **xylem** and **phloem**; all labelled.

(b) In dry weather the **bulliform cells lose water** and become flaccid, so the upper surface **shrinks** and the blade **rolls inwards**, which **reduces** the surface exposed and so the loss of **water vapour**.
